 <ORGANISATION> - <ROLE>

Critical Non-Compliance Indicators
   ●​ Lack of Reproducibility. Failure to execute the solution following README instructions.
   ●​ Code-writeup mismatch. The writeup describes features, architecture, or results that do not
       match what is in the repo.
   ●​ Insufficient Technical Justification. Candidates must be able to articulate the technical
       rationale behind their code and architecture during subsequent interviews.
   ●​ Unsubstantiated Model Selection. Model choices must be justified by operational requirements
       such as data privacy, latency, or specific task suitability.
   ●​ Substandard Code Quality. While AI-assisted coding is permitted, the final output must meet
       professional standards for code quality and maintainability.
   ●​ Recycling a Past Project. Candidates must start a fresh project. If we have reasonable doubt of
       you recycling your capstone project (for example), you may be disqualified without justification.



Approved Methodologies and Resources
   ●​ Tool Selection. Candidates may utilize any accessible AI tools, including open-source weights
       and local inference. Organization-provided API keys or compute resources will not be issued.
       Submissions should clearly state any technical limitations and describe potential enhancements
       if those constraints were removed.
   ●​ Resource Accessibility. Solutions should be functional within free-tier resource limits. If the
       prototype requires paid infrastructure for production scale, this should be noted in the
      documentation.
   ●​ Usage of AI and coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, etc) is permitted. What
       we evaluate is the final artifact and your ability to explain the decisions in it. If you used coding
       agents, please include a section at the end of your README on how you have used them to
       support your work. In addition, upload all coding agent session and chat logs (e.g. jsonl from
       ~/.claude/projects/) to your repository and indicate their location in your README.
   ●​ Local vs API models does not matter. What matters is that you can justify the choice on
       grounds that hold up (data sensitivity, latency, task fit, fine-tuning needs, cost-at-scale
       economics). Not on grounds that do not (free, cool, had it lying around).
   ●​ Free resources if you are starting from scratch. LLM APIs: Google AI Studio, Groq, OpenRouter,
       Hugging Face Inference Providers, Cerebras, Together AI. Local inference: Ollama, llama.cpp,
       LM Studio. GPU compute: Google Colab, Kaggle Notebooks, Lightning AI. Open weights and
       datasets: Hugging Face, Kaggle.




Supplemental Guidance
   ●​ Annex A (below): around 21 problem statement sketches drawn from real public-sector work,
       anonymised. Pick one, remix one, or ignore them all, completely up to you. They are here to
      calibrate the shape of the space, not to constrain you.
   ●​ Annex B: {build} 2025 public projects. Past <ORGANISATION> hackathon submissions. Not all AI-focused,
       but a good sense of what real shipped prototypes look like in this environment, given a
       month-long window.
 <ORGANISATION> - <ROLE>

Annex A. Example problem sketches
Paraphrased and anonymised. They are here to show you the shape of the space, not to restrict you.


Vision, video, and multimodal understanding
  1.​ Property condition assessment from imagery. A government tax agency assesses the
      construction era and condition of residential properties for valuation. Today officers eyeball
      street-level imagery, which is subjective, slow, and inconsistent across valuers. Could a vision
      model compress turnaround and improve consistency?

  2.​ Structured attribute extraction from animal photos. A community ecosystem management
      programme needs to extract attributes from photos of stray animals, such as sterilisation status
      (via ear-tipping), gender, and approximate age. Could a vision model do this reliably enough to
      support routine operations?

  3.​ Urban disamenity detection from imagery. Municipal issues like illegal dumping, overgrown
      greenery, or damaged infrastructure can be flagged from images submitted by officers or
      citizens. Could a VLM produce structured outputs (category, severity, location cues) from
      photos, with a real precision/recall eval?


Retrieval & knowledge
  4.​ Precedent-aware response drafting. Officers have tight deadlines to draft responses to
      legislative or ministerial questions. The work requires precedent from past replies, press
      releases, speeches, and policy documents scattered across repositories. How might you
      compress the research phase so drafting gets the focus?

  5.​ Benefits matching for citizens. Across dozens of government schemes, citizens may be
      eligible for many they do not know about. Existing portals are searchable but passive: the
      citizen does the discovery. Could a profile-driven matcher proactively surface entitlements?

  6.​ Legal evidence navigation. Court bundles can run thousands of pages. Judges and legal
      teams need to find specific facts, arguments, and inconsistencies. Could you build something
      that lets them query evidence without hallucinating claims that are not in the record?


Generation with guardrails
  7.​ Document-to-presentation. A common public-sector workflow: take a long policy document,
      produce a presentation for leadership. Could an AI system produce editable slides that match
      organisational conventions and actually communicate the substance?

  8.​ Targeted practice questions. Students and parents want practice questions aligned to
      syllabus and specific topics. Existing options are generic or expensive. Could you generate
      practice that is both aligned and pedagogically sound, with an eval for correctness and difficulty
      calibration?

  9.​ Synthetic data for data-scarce vision tasks. Some detection tasks lack enough real training
      data, such as oil spills, rare safety violations, or culturally specific artefacts. Could you generate
      synthetic visual data and show empirically that models pre-conditioned on it transfer to real
      data?
 <ORGANISATION> - <ROLE>

Agents & multi-step workflows
  10.​Feedback-to-ticket pipeline. Product teams receive user feedback. Humans read it, group it,
      write specs, brief engineers. Could an agent system handle the first mile (triaging, clustering,
      drafting tickets) without losing signal?

  11.​ Automated safety testing for LLM apps. Given an LLM application endpoint, an agent
       generates adversarial prompts, probes for jailbreaks, and produces a structured safety report.
       Signal is in how you generate good adversarial prompts, not the plumbing.

  12.​Triage agent for citizen emails. Agencies receive high volumes of emails covering many use
      cases against complex internal SOPs. Could an agent read the email, classify it, look up the
      relevant SOP, and draft a response, with calibrated confidence and clean human escalation?


Evaluation, benchmarking, robustness
  13.​AI output quality harness. AI-generated content is flooding workflows and quality is
      inconsistent. How might you build a lightweight eval harness that catches low-quality AI output
      before it reaches readers, without being so strict it blocks good output?

  14.​Localised safety benchmark. Existing LLM safety benchmarks are mostly US-centric. Could
      you construct and validate a small benchmark that tests for Singapore-specific context
      (Singlish, local slang, local references) and use it to evaluate at least two off-the-shelf models
      honestly?

  15.​Out-of-knowledge-base robustness. RAG systems often confabulate when asked questions
      their knowledge base cannot answer. Could you build a small benchmark and eval tool that
      measures how often a RAG system acknowledges “I do not know” vs. makes things up?




Annex B. {build} 2025 public projects
https://build.tech.gov.sg/projects/2025. Browse for a sense of what past <ORGANISATION> hackathon
submissions look like. Not all AI-focused, but a useful calibration for what “reasonable scope shipped in a
short window” means in this environment.

The important distinction is: **the assessment does not explicitly require judge–human agreement**. It requires you to select and justify an evaluation methodology, listing benchmarking, LLM-as-judge, human evaluation, ablation, and comparison as examples. It also says evaluation soundness matters more than headline scores and allocates 30% to evaluation. :codex-file-citation{path="<REPOSITORY>\<SCRATCHPAD>\<ASSESSMENT_BRIEF>.pdf" purpose="source"}

Judge–human agreement became necessary because **your project chose an LLM judge and promised to validate it against humans**.

## What the evaluation includes

### 1. Freeze the evaluated system

Fix the:

- Gemini drafting model
- Draft prompt
- Groundedness-judge prompt
- Routing thresholds
- Evaluation sample and random seed

This prevents changing the prompt after seeing disappointing results.

### 2. Generate approximately 50 drafts

Sample from emails automated at the frozen operating point, covering:

- Auto-replies
- Redirects
- Different predicted topics
- Multi-SOP cases
- Different confidence levels

Only successful drafts enter the quality evaluation. Failed API calls remain in the separate **drafting availability** metric.

For example, if 50 drafts are attempted but 42 succeed:

- Drafting availability: `42/50 = 84%`
- Human evaluation denominator: `42`
- The eight missing drafts are not incorrectly labelled “bad drafts”

### 3. Give humans and the LLM judge identical evidence

Each reviewer receives:

- Redacted citizen email
- All SOPs supplied to the drafter
- Redacted draft reply

The human sheet hides:

- LLM judge verdict
- Model confidence
- Classifier prediction
- True class
- Original email/scenario identity

That blinding prevents the reviewer from unconsciously agreeing with the system.

### 4. Humans apply the rubric

Your current protocol asks humans to rate:

| Dimension | Question |
|---|---|
| Groundedness | Are all factual claims supported by the SOP or attributed to the citizen? |
| Correct next step | Does the response give an appropriate SOP-supported action or destination? |
| Safety/privacy | Does it avoid disclosure, fabricated identifiers, unsafe advice, and unsupported commitments? |
| Completeness | Does it cover the material parts of the enquiry? |
| Tone | Is it clear, respectful, neutral public-service language? |
| Overall acceptability | Could an officer send it after ordinary proofreading without correcting its substance? |

An ungrounded or unsafe draft is automatically an overall rejection.

The LLM judge currently evaluates **only groundedness**. Therefore:

- Human ratings measure overall draft quality.
- Judge–human agreement compares only the groundedness label.
- You should not claim the judge validates tone, completeness, or safety.

The exact rubric is in [HUMAN_EVAL.md](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md:28>).

### 5. Use independent reviewers

Your implemented protocol requires:

- Reviewer A evaluates every successful draft.
- Reviewer B evaluates at least 20 drafts or 30% of the sample, whichever is larger.
- Every disagreement or `UNSURE` result receives separate adjudication.

For 50 successful drafts, that means:

- Reviewer A: 50
- Reviewer B: 20
- Adjudicator: only disagreements

You can be Reviewer A. Reviewer B should ideally be someone who did not build the system.

### 6. Report the results

The scorer produces:

- Human acceptance and per-dimension pass rates
- 95% Wilson confidence intervals
- Human–human raw agreement
- Human–human Cohen’s κ
- Judge–human agreement
- Judge–human Cohen’s κ
- Groundedness confusion matrix
- Judge recall for human-identified ungrounded drafts
- Judge precision when it flags a draft
- Separate agreement for auto-replies and redirects
- Missing-judgment and unresolved-disagreement counts

The most important judge metric is:

> Of the drafts humans considered ungrounded, how many did the LLM judge catch?

A judge could achieve 90% overall agreement simply by calling nearly everything grounded. That is why ungrounded recall and the confusion matrix matter more than agreement alone.

## Where your project made it necessary

Your own documents establish the commitment:

- [README evaluation methodology](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/README.md:197>) says the LLM judge requires blinded human comparison.
- [BUILD.md](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/<SCRATCHPAD>/BUILD.md:583>) promises that the same drafts will be reviewed by hand and agreement reported.
- [drafting.py](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/eval/drafting.py:20>) describes agreement as what makes the judge defensible rather than decorative.
- [README limitations](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/README.md:395>) correctly admits that human labels have not yet been collected.

Therefore, you have three choices:

1. **Complete the study — recommended.** This fulfils your stated methodology and strengthens the highest-weight rubric category.
2. Remove the LLM judge and report a human-only draft evaluation.
3. Submit with the study declared incomplete, which is honest but leaves a prominent evaluation gap.

Given the competitive bar, I recommend completing it. Once Gemini quota resets, the work should take roughly **60–90 minutes for the primary review, 20–30 minutes for the second reviewer, and 10–20 minutes for adjudication and reporting**.

ok, and this report result is done once and saved where?

Yes—run it once against the frozen model, prompts, thresholds, and sample, then commit the evidence.

Files are saved as:

- `eval/results/drafts.json` — generated drafts and LLM-judge verdicts
- `eval/results/drafting.json` — availability and grounding summary
- `eval/human_review/manifest.json` — sealed sample mapping and evidence hashes
- `eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv` — primary human ratings
- `eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv` — independent overlap ratings
- `eval/human_review/adjudicated.csv` — disagreements, if any
- **`eval/results/judge_human_agreement.json` — final report**

Currently, `judge_human_agreement.json` says `status: "not_run"` because Gemini produced no drafts under the current rate limit.

After the reviewer CSVs are completed, generate the final report with:

```powershell
python eval/human_review.py score `
  --ratings eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv `
  --adjudication eval/human_review/adjudicated.csv
```

The scoring step makes no API calls, so it can be rerun safely while correcting annotation errors. Once it reports `status: "complete"`, commit the report, manifest, and anonymised rating CSVs.

You only need to repeat the entire evaluation if you change the drafter model, drafting prompt, judge model/prompt, routing thresholds, or evaluation sample.

def _judge_agreement(
    manifest_items: list[dict[str, Any]], references: dict[str, dict[str, str]]
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    comparable = [
        item
        for item in manifest_items
        if item.get("judge_verdict") in {"GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED"}
        and item["item_id"] in references
    ]
    human = [references[str(item["item_id"])]["groundedness"] for item in comparable]
    judge = [str(item["judge_verdict"]) for item in comparable]
    report = _agreement(human, judge, ("GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED"))

    human_ungrounded = sum(value == "UNGROUNDED" for value in human)
    judge_ungrounded = sum(value == "UNGROUNDED" for value in judge)
    caught = sum(
        want == "UNGROUNDED" and got == "UNGROUNDED"
        for want, got in zip(human, judge, strict=True)
    )
    true_ungrounded = caught
    report.update({
        "human_ungrounded": human_ungrounded,
        "judge_ungrounded": judge_ungrounded,
        "ungrounded_recall": (
            round(caught / human_ungrounded, 4) if human_ungrounded else None
        ),
        "ungrounded_precision": (
            round(true_ungrounded / judge_ungrounded, 4) if judge_ungrounded else None
        ),
        "note": (
            "Human labels are the reference. Ungrounded recall is the safety-critical "
            "quantity: it is the share of human-identified unsupported drafts the "
            "judge also catches."
        ),
    })

    by_route: dict[str, Any] = {}
    for route in sorted({str(item.get("route", "unknown")) for item in comparable}):
        subset = [item for item in comparable if str(item.get("route", "unknown")) == route]
        route_human = [references[str(item["item_id"])]["groundedness"] for item in subset]
        route_judge = [str(item["judge_verdict"]) for item in subset]
        by_route[route] = _agreement(
            route_human, route_judge, ("GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED")
        )
    report["by_route"] = by_route
    return report


def score_reviews(
    manifest_path: Path,
    rating_paths: list[Path],
    output_path: Path,
    *,
    adjudication_path: Path | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Validate human labels and write the agreement/quality report."""
    manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    manifest_items = list(manifest.get("items") or ())
    evidence_by_item = {
        str(item["item_id"]): str(item.get("evidence_sha256", ""))
        for item in manifest_items
    }
    if any(not value for value in evidence_by_item.values()):
        raise ValueError("manifest is missing per-item evidence hashes")
    ratings = _load_ratings(rating_paths, evidence_by_item)
    adjudications = (
        _load_ratings([adjudication_path], evidence_by_item)
        if adjudication_path is not None
        else []
    )
    references, unresolved = _resolve_references(
        manifest_items, ratings, adjudications
    )

    ratings_by_item: dict[str, list[Rating]] = defaultdict(list)
    for rating in ratings:
        ratings_by_item[rating.item_id].append(rating)
    double_reviewed = sum(len(values) >= 2 for values in ratings_by_item.values())
    target = int(manifest.get("protocol", {}).get("double_review_target", 0))
    reviewer_ids = sorted({rating.reviewer_id for rating in ratings})

    quality_labels = {
        "groundedness": "GROUNDED",
        "correct_next_step": "PASS",
        "safety_privacy": "PASS",
        "completeness": "PASS",
        "tone": "PASS",
        "overall_acceptability": "ACCEPT",
    }
    human_quality = {
        field: _wilson(
            sum(values[field] == success for values in references.values()),
            len(references),
        )
        for field, success in quality_labels.items()
    }

    judged = sum(
        item.get("judge_verdict") in {"GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED"}
        for item in manifest_items
    )
    complete_conditions = {
        "all_successful_drafts_judged": judged == len(manifest_items),
        "all_successful_drafts_human_reviewed": len(references) == len(manifest_items),
        "no_unresolved_fields": not unresolved,
        "at_least_two_reviewers": len(reviewer_ids) >= 2,
        "double_review_target_met": double_reviewed >= target,
    }
    complete = all(complete_conditions.values())
    report = {
        "generated_at": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "status": "complete" if complete else "incomplete",
        "source": manifest.get("source", {}),
        "protocol": manifest.get("protocol", {}),
        "coverage": {
            "successful_drafts": len(manifest_items),
            "judge_verdicts": judged,
            "human_reference_labels": len(references),
            "reviewers": reviewer_ids,
            "double_reviewed": double_reviewed,
            "double_review_target": target,
            "unresolved": unresolved,
            "complete_conditions": complete_conditions,
        },
        "human_quality": human_quality,
        "inter_human_reliability": _pairwise_reliability(ratings),
        "judge_human_groundedness": _judge_agreement(manifest_items, references),
        "interpretation": (
            "The human reference is authoritative. Single-reviewed items use that "
            "reviewer's label; matching double reviews use their consensus; any "
            "disagreement or UNSURE value requires a separate adjudication row. "
            "Wilson intervals show denominator uncertainty for human quality rates."
        ),
        "limitations": [
            "Reviewers see synthetic correspondence and authored SOPs, not real inbox mail.",
            "Agreement validates this judge prompt and sample, not arbitrary future prompts.",
            "A sample with no human-identified ungrounded draft cannot estimate judge recall.",
        ],
    }
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    output_path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return report


def _parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    commands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    prepare = commands.add_parser("prepare", help="write a blinded reviewer CSV")

    score.add_argument("--adjudication", type=Path, default=None)
    score.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_REPORT)
    return parser

**5.3 Ablations.** Three, each isolating one design claim: does calibration change any
*decision* or only the ECE; do per-bucket thresholds beat one global number; does
scrubbing PII cost accuracy.

**5.4 Comparison.** Fine-tuned encoder vs LLM zero-shot with self-consistency, on the
same stratified sample with a **fixed label set** for both (deriving the label set from
the data makes the two macro-F1 figures averages over different denominators — a
0.11–0.22 discrepancy on identical predictions).

**5.5 LLM-as-judge — protocol ready, labels outstanding.** A Groq-hosted judge scores
draft groundedness, deliberately a different model family from the drafter. The judge
and reviewers now receive the same redacted email, SOPs and draft; blinded reviewer
sheets omit the judge verdict, classifier output, confidence and ground truth. One
reviewer covers every successful draft and a second independently covers at least 20
items or 30%, with disagreements adjudicated separately. The scorer reports raw
agreement, Cohen's κ, a confusion matrix and judge recall on human-identified
unsupported drafts. The protocol is `eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md`. **Human labels have not yet
been collected, so no groundedness or agreement number is claimed here.** The
machine-readable status is `eval/results/judge_human_agreement.json`.

**5.6 Uncertainty.** Every headline interval is a 95% percentile bootstrap over 2,000
resamples. The resampling unit is the whole authored scenario, not an individual email
variant, and resampling occurs within true-class strata to preserve the balanced
benchmark design. This reflects variation among the 36 observed test scenarios; it
does not measure synthetic-data bias, deployment shift, or unseen situations.

---

## 6. Results

python -m pytest                    # 400 tests
python eval/run_eval.py --no-draft  # regenerates committed offline results
streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py
```

Run `python eval/run_eval.py` without `--no-draft` only when you intend to spend
Gemini/Groq quota on the sampled drafting and judge evaluation.

After that live run, prepare independent human review sheets and score them without
making another API call:

```bash
python eval/human_review.py prepare --reviewer-id reviewer_a --output eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv
python eval/human_review.py prepare --reviewer-id reviewer_b --overlap-only --output eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv
python eval/human_review.py score --ratings eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv
```

The complete rating rubric, blinding rule and adjudication procedure are in
`eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md`.

Or run the same demo in Docker:

```bash
docker build -t citizen-triage-agent .
docker run --rm -p 8501:8501 --env-file .env citizen-triage-agent
```

**The pipeline runs with no API key at all.** Classification, calibration, retrieval
and routing are entirely local. A missing or rate-limited key means every auto-reply
records a drafting failure and escalates *carrying its SOP* — the designed path, not a
crash.

**Free-tier note.** Gemini's free drafting quota is a *daily* budget. `.env` supports
`GEMINI_API_KEY_2` and `_3`; the client rotates on 429 and continues. Rotation fires
only on rate limit — a timeout would fail identically on the next key.

---

## 8. Limitations

Stated rather than defended away.

- **The judge–human agreement figure is not computed**, so no groundedness number is
  claimed. The blinded review, double-rating, adjudication and scoring workflow is
  implemented and tested, but `eval/results/drafting.json` still reads
  `{"skipped": true}` because the live draft/judge sample has not been run and humans
  have not supplied labels.
- **Calibration is currently a near-no-op** (T=0.998). See §6.4.
- **Scam detection is the weakest guarantee.** The lexical flag has precision 1.000
  (zero false positives on all 3,000 emails), but recall is **0.827 corpus-wide** —
  not the 0.952 the test split alone reports. The 52 misses describe the *event*
  without ever naming it ("a man called saying I'd be arrested"), and the most
  distressed citizen is the least likely to write "scam". An LLM second pass is the
  right instrument; regex cannot reach these. Note this bounds *misfile* risk only: a
  correctly classified scam report escalates on its bucket without consulting the flag.
- **PII scrubbing is regex + gazetteer**, deliberately a stand-in for an offline NER
  model. Recall is 1.000 on *planted* values — which measures detection of shapes the
  generator knew to plant, not of everything a citizen might write. Addresses with
  neither a block number nor a street-type token are unreachable; conversely

**5.3 Ablations.** Three, each isolating one design claim: does calibration change any
*decision* or only the ECE; do per-bucket thresholds beat one global number; does
scrubbing PII cost accuracy.

**5.4 Comparison.** Fine-tuned encoder vs LLM zero-shot with self-consistency, on the
same stratified sample with a **fixed label set** for both (deriving the label set from
the data makes the two macro-F1 figures averages over different denominators — a
0.11–0.22 discrepancy on identical predictions).

**5.5 LLM-as-judge — protocol ready, labels outstanding.** A Groq-hosted judge scores
draft groundedness, deliberately a different model family from the drafter. The judge
and reviewers now receive the same redacted email, SOPs and draft; blinded reviewer
sheets omit the judge verdict, classifier output, confidence and ground truth. One
reviewer covers every successful draft and a second independently covers at least 20
items or 30%, with disagreements adjudicated separately. The scorer reports raw
agreement, Cohen's κ, a confusion matrix and judge recall on human-identified
unsupported drafts. The protocol is `eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md`. **Human labels have not yet
been collected, so no groundedness or agreement number is claimed here.** The
machine-readable status is `eval/results/judge_human_agreement.json`.

**5.6 Uncertainty.** Every headline interval is a 95% percentile bootstrap over 2,000
resamples. The resampling unit is the whole authored scenario, not an individual email
variant, and resampling occurs within true-class strata to preserve the balanced
benchmark design. This reflects variation among the 36 observed test scenarios; it
does not measure synthetic-data bias, deployment shift, or unseen situations.

# Calibrated Triage for Citizen Correspondence

A triage agent for a tax authority's individual-income-tax inbox. It reads a
citizen's email, classifies the intent, looks up the governing internal procedure,
and either drafts a grounded reply or escalates to an officer with a stated reason.

**The contribution is not the drafting. It is knowing when not to draft.**

> **Demo video:** _[URL to be added before submission]_

---

## 1. The problem

An agency inbox is not one problem. It is a mixture of questions that a published
FAQ already answers, questions that require reading a specific taxpayer's record,
and questions where a wrong answer causes real harm — a citizen mid-fraud, or one
who cannot pay.

The naive framing is "use an LLM to answer citizen emails". That framing fails on
the only question an agency actually has, which is not *can it draft?* but:

> **What share of this inbox can I safely automate, and at what error rate?**

That is a coverage/risk trade-off, and it is a curve rather than a number. A system
that answers 100% of emails at 15% error is unusable in a public-sector context; one
that answers 35% at 9% error, and hands the rest to a human *with a reason attached*,
is deployable. This project is built around producing and defending that curve.

This is Annex A sketch 12 (triage agent for citizen emails), taken deliberately at
its hardest reading: **calibrated confidence and clean human escalation**, not
autocomplete for officers.

---

## 2. What it does

```
  mock inbox (JSON)
        |
        v
  1. PII SCRUB ......... local regex + gazetteer; placeholders substituted
        |                BEFORE any external call
        v
  2. CLASSIFIER ........ MiniLM-L6, fine-tuned, 10 classes, local CPU
        |
        v
  3. BUCKET ROLLUP ..... 10 classes -> 5 routing buckets
        |
        v
  4. CALIBRATION ....... temperature scaling on the bucket distribution
        |
        v
  5. SOP LOOKUP ........ CLASS_TO_SOPS[class] from SOP frontmatter
        |                no vector search, no embeddings
        v
  6. ROUTER ............ decide(bucket, calibrated confidence, flags)
        |
        +---> AUTO-REPLY .... Gemini, grounded in the retrieved SOP
        +---> REDIRECT ...... out-of-scope, still SOP-grounded

`tests/test_runtime_is_free.py` was removed. It had scanned `src/` imports to prove

writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.

fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:

    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")

    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

)

    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

       grounds that hold up (data sensitivity, latency, task fit, fine-tuning needs, cost-at-scale
       economics). Not on grounds that do not (free, cool, had it lying around).
   ●​ Free resources if you are starting from scratch. LLM APIs: Google AI Studio, Groq, OpenRouter,
       Hugging Face Inference Providers, Cerebras, Together AI. Local inference: Ollama, llama.cpp,
       LM Studio. GPU compute: Google Colab, Kaggle Notebooks, Lightning AI. Open weights and
       datasets: Hugging Face, Kaggle.




Supplemental Guidance
   ●​ Annex A (below): around 21 problem statement sketches drawn from real public-sector work,
       anonymised. Pick one, remix one, or ignore them all, completely up to you. They are here to
      calibrate the shape of the space, not to constrain you.
   ●​ Annex B: {build} 2025 public projects. Past <ORGANISATION> hackathon submissions. Not all AI-focused,
       but a good sense of what real shipped prototypes look like in this environment, given a
       month-long window.
 <ORGANISATION> - <ROLE>

Annex A. Example problem sketches
Paraphrased and anonymised. They are here to show you the shape of the space, not to restrict you.


Vision, video, and multimodal understanding
  1.​ Property condition assessment from imagery. A government tax agency assesses the
      construction era and condition of residential properties for valuation. Today officers eyeball
      street-level imagery, which is subjective, slow, and inconsistent across valuers. Could a vision
      model compress turnaround and improve consistency?

  2.​ Structured attribute extraction from animal photos. A community ecosystem management
      programme needs to extract attributes from photos of stray animals, such as sterilisation status
      (via ear-tipping), gender, and approximate age. Could a vision model do this reliably enough to
      support routine operations?

  3.​ Urban disamenity detection from imagery. Municipal issues like illegal dumping, overgrown
      greenery, or damaged infrastructure can be flagged from images submitted by officers or
      citizens. Could a VLM produce structured outputs (category, severity, location cues) from
      photos, with a real precision/recall eval?


Retrieval & knowledge
  4.​ Precedent-aware response drafting. Officers have tight deadlines to draft responses to
      legislative or ministerial questions. The work requires precedent from past replies, press
      releases, speeches, and policy documents scattered across repositories. How might you
      compress the research phase so drafting gets the focus?

  5.​ Benefits matching for citizens. Across dozens of government schemes, citizens may be
      eligible for many they do not know about. Existing portals are searchable but passive: the
      citizen does the discovery. Could a profile-driven matcher proactively surface entitlements?

  6.​ Legal evidence navigation. Court bundles can run thousands of pages. Judges and legal
      teams need to find specific facts, arguments, and inconsistencies. Could you build something
      that lets them query evidence without hallucinating claims that are not in the record?


Generation with guardrails
  7.​ Document-to-presentation. A common public-sector workflow: take a long policy document,
      produce a presentation for leadership. Could an AI system produce editable slides that match
      organisational conventions and actually communicate the substance?

  8.​ Targeted practice questions. Students and parents want practice questions aligned to
      syllabus and specific topics. Existing options are generic or expensive. Could you generate
      practice that is both aligned and pedagogically sound, with an eval for correctness and difficulty
      calibration?

  9.​ Synthetic data for data-scarce vision tasks. Some detection tasks lack enough real training
      data, such as oil spills, rare safety violations, or culturally specific artefacts. Could you generate
      synthetic visual data and show empirically that models pre-conditioned on it transfer to real
      data?
 <ORGANISATION> - <ROLE>

Agents & multi-step workflows
  10.​Feedback-to-ticket pipeline. Product teams receive user feedback. Humans read it, group it,
      write specs, brief engineers. Could an agent system handle the first mile (triaging, clustering,
      drafting tickets) without losing signal?

  11.​ Automated safety testing for LLM apps. Given an LLM application endpoint, an agent
       generates adversarial prompts, probes for jailbreaks, and produces a structured safety report.
       Signal is in how you generate good adversarial prompts, not the plumbing.

  12.​Triage agent for citizen emails. Agencies receive high volumes of emails covering many use
      cases against complex internal SOPs. Could an agent read the email, classify it, look up the
      relevant SOP, and draft a response, with calibrated confidence and clean human escalation?


Evaluation, benchmarking, robustness
  13.​AI output quality harness. AI-generated content is flooding workflows and quality is
      inconsistent. How might you build a lightweight eval harness that catches low-quality AI output
      before it reaches readers, without being so strict it blocks good output?

  14.​Localised safety benchmark. Existing LLM safety benchmarks are mostly US-centric. Could
      you construct and validate a small benchmark that tests for Singapore-specific context
      (Singlish, local slang, local references) and use it to evaluate at least two off-the-shelf models
      honestly?

  15.​Out-of-knowledge-base robustness. RAG systems often confabulate when asked questions
      their knowledge base cannot answer. Could you build a small benchmark and eval tool that
      measures how often a RAG system acknowledges “I do not know” vs. makes things up?

submissions look like. Not all AI-focused, but a useful calibration for what “reasonable scope shipped in a
short window” means in this environment.

content.text:
The important distinction is: **the assessment does not explicitly require judge–human agreement**. It requires you to select and justify an evaluation methodology, listing benchmarking, LLM-as-judge, human evaluation, ablation, and comparison as examples. It also says evaluation soundness matters more than headline scores and allocates 30% to evaluation. :codex-file-citation{path="<REPOSITORY>\<SCRATCHPAD>\<ASSESSMENT_BRIEF>.pdf" purpose="source"}

Judge–human agreement became necessary because **your project chose an LLM judge and promised to validate it against humans**.

## What the evaluation includes

### 1. Freeze the evaluated system

Fix the:

- Gemini drafting model
- Draft prompt
- Groundedness-judge prompt
- Routing thresholds
- Evaluation sample and random seed

This prevents changing the prompt after seeing disappointing results.

### 2. Generate approximately 50 drafts

Sample from emails automated at the frozen operating point, covering:

- Auto-replies
- Redirects
- Different predicted topics
- Multi-SOP cases
- Different confidence levels

Only successful drafts enter the quality evaluation. Failed API calls remain in the separate **drafting availability** metric.

For example, if 50 drafts are attempted but 42 succeed:

- Drafting availability: `42/50 = 84%`
- Human evaluation denominator: `42`
- The eight missing drafts are not incorrectly labelled “bad drafts”

### 3. Give humans and the LLM judge identical evidence

Each reviewer receives:

- Redacted citizen email
- All SOPs supplied to the drafter
- Redacted draft reply

The human sheet hides:

- LLM judge verdict
- Model confidence
- Classifier prediction
- True class
- Original email/scenario identity

That blinding prevents the reviewer from unconsciously agreeing with the system.

### 4. Humans apply the rubric

Your current protocol asks humans to rate:

| Dimension | Question |
|---|---|
| Groundedness | Are all factual claims supported by the SOP or attributed to the citizen? |
| Correct next step | Does the response give an appropriate SOP-supported action or destination? |
| Safety/privacy | Does it avoid disclosure, fabricated identifiers, unsafe advice, and unsupported commitments? |
| Completeness | Does it cover the material parts of the enquiry? |
| Tone | Is it clear, respectful, neutral public-service language? |
| Overall acceptability | Could an officer send it after ordinary proofreading without correcting its substance? |

An ungrounded or unsafe draft is automatically an overall rejection.

The LLM judge currently evaluates **only groundedness**. Therefore:

- Human ratings measure overall draft quality.
- Judge–human agreement compares only the groundedness label.
- You should not claim the judge validates tone, completeness, or safety.

The exact rubric is in [HUMAN_EVAL.md](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md:28>).

### 5. Use independent reviewers

Your implemented protocol requires:

- Reviewer A evaluates every successful draft.
- Reviewer B evaluates at least 20 drafts or 30% of the sample, whichever is larger.
- Every disagreement or `UNSURE` result receives separate adjudication.

For 50 successful drafts, that means:

- Reviewer A: 50
- Reviewer B: 20
- Adjudicator: only disagreements

You can be Reviewer A. Reviewer B should ideally be someone who did not build the system.

### 6. Report the results

The scorer produces:

- Human acceptance and per-dimension pass rates
- 95% Wilson confidence intervals
- Human–human raw agreement
- Human–human Cohen’s κ
- Judge–human agreement
- Judge–human Cohen’s κ
- Groundedness confusion matrix
- Judge recall for human-identified ungrounded drafts
- Judge precision when it flags a draft
- Separate agreement for auto-replies and redirects
- Missing-judgment and unresolved-disagreement counts

The most important judge metric is:

> Of the drafts humans considered ungrounded, how many did the LLM judge catch?

A judge could achieve 90% overall agreement simply by calling nearly everything grounded. That is why ungrounded recall and the confusion matrix matter more than agreement alone.

## Where your project made it necessary

Your own documents establish the commitment:

- [README evaluation methodology](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/README.md:197>) says the LLM judge requires blinded human comparison.
- [BUILD.md](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/<SCRATCHPAD>/BUILD.md:583>) promises that the same drafts will be reviewed by hand and agreement reported.
- [drafting.py](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/eval/drafting.py:20>) describes agreement as what makes the judge defensible rather than decorative.
- [README limitations](</C:/Users/<USER>/Documents/all ur code projects/bojji/README.md:395>) correctly admits that human labels have not yet been collected.

Therefore, you have three choices:

1. **Complete the study — recommended.** This fulfils your stated methodology and strengthens the highest-weight rubric category.
2. Remove the LLM judge and report a human-only draft evaluation.
3. Submit with the study declared incomplete, which is honest but leaves a prominent evaluation gap.

Given the competitive bar, I recommend completing it. Once Gemini quota resets, the work should take roughly **60–90 minutes for the primary review, 20–30 minutes for the second reviewer, and 10–20 minutes for adjudication and reporting**.
ok, and this report result is done once and saved where?

Yes—run it once against the frozen model, prompts, thresholds, and sample, then commit the evidence.

Files are saved as:

- `eval/results/drafts.json` — generated drafts and LLM-judge verdicts
- `eval/results/drafting.json` — availability and grounding summary
- `eval/human_review/manifest.json` — sealed sample mapping and evidence hashes
- `eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv` — primary human ratings
- `eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv` — independent overlap ratings
- `eval/human_review/adjudicated.csv` — disagreements, if any
- **`eval/results/judge_human_agreement.json` — final report**

Currently, `judge_human_agreement.json` says `status: "not_run"` because Gemini produced no drafts under the current rate limit.

After the reviewer CSVs are completed, generate the final report with:

```powershell
python eval/human_review.py score `
  --ratings eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv `
  --adjudication eval/human_review/adjudicated.csv
```

The scoring step makes no API calls, so it can be rerun safely while correcting annotation errors. Once it reports `status: "complete"`, commit the report, manifest, and anonymised rating CSVs.

You only need to repeat the entire evaluation if you change the drafter model, drafting prompt, judge model/prompt, routing thresholds, or evaluation sample.

def _display_rate(value: Any) -> str:

def render_markdown_report(report: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """Render the machine-readable result as the README-facing report."""
    coverage = report["coverage"]
    human_quality = report["human_quality"]
    agreement = report["judge_human_groundedness"]
    complete = report["status"] == "complete"

    lines = [
        "# Human draft evaluation and judge agreement",
        "",
        f"**Status: {str(report['status']).upper()}**",
        "",
    ]
    if not complete:
        lines.extend([
            "> This report is incomplete. It must not be cited as evidence of draft",
            "> quality or judge validity until every completion condition passes.",
            "",
        ])
    lines.extend([
        f"Generated: `{report['generated_at']}`",
        "",
        "## Evaluation coverage",
        "",
        "| Quantity | Count |",
        "|---|---:|",
        f"| Successful drafts | {coverage['successful_drafts']} |",
        f"| LLM-judge verdicts | {coverage['judge_verdicts']} |",
        f"| Resolved human references | {coverage['human_reference_labels']} |",
        f"| Independently double-reviewed | {coverage['double_reviewed']} |",
        f"| Required double-review target | {coverage['double_review_target']} |",
        "",
        "Completion checks:",
        "",
    ])
    for name, passed in coverage["complete_conditions"].items():
        label = name.replace("_", " ")
        lines.append(f"- {'PASS' if passed else 'PENDING'} â€” {label}")

    lines.extend([
        "",
        "## Human draft-quality ratings",
        "",
        "Humans are the reference. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals for the",
        "observed sample proportions.",
        "",
        "| Dimension | Passing | Rate | 95% interval |",
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|",
    ])
    for field, metric in human_quality.items():
        label = field.replace("_", " ").title()
        interval = f"{_display_rate(metric['lower'])}â€“{_display_rate(metric['upper'])}"
        lines.append(
            f"| {label} | {metric['successes']}/{metric['n']} | "
            f"{_display_rate(metric['rate'])} | {interval} |"
        )

    lines.extend([
        "",
        "## LLM judge versus human groundedness",
        "",
        "| Metric | Result |",
        "|---|---:|",
        f"| Comparable items | {agreement['n']} |",
        f"| Raw agreement | {_display_rate(agreement['rate'])} |",
        f"| Cohen's Îº | {_display_number(agreement['cohen_kappa'])} |",
        f"| Human-identified ungrounded drafts | {agreement['human_ungrounded']} |",
        f"| Judge ungrounded recall | {_display_rate(agreement['ungrounded_recall'])} |",
        f"| Judge ungrounded precision | {_display_rate(agreement['ungrounded_precision'])} |",
        "",
        "Confusion matrix (rows are human reference; columns are LLM judge):",
        "",
        "| Human \\ Judge | Grounded | Ungrounded |",
        "|---|---:|---:|",
    ])
    confusion = agreement["confusion_rows_reference_columns_comparison"]
    for human in ("GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED"):
        lines.append(
            f"| {human.title()} | {confusion[human]['GROUNDED']} | "
            f"{confusion[human]['UNGROUNDED']} |"
        )

    lines.extend(["", "Agreement by route:", ""])
    lines.extend([
        "| Route | Comparable items | Agreement | Cohen's Îº |",
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|",
    ])
    for route, metric in agreement["by_route"].items():
        lines.append(
            f"| {route} | {metric['n']} | {_display_rate(metric['rate'])} | "
            f"{_display_number(metric['cohen_kappa'])} |"
        )

    lines.extend(["", "## Inter-human reliability", ""])
    pairs = report["inter_human_reliability"]
    if pairs:
        lines.extend([
            "| Reviewers | Overlap | Groundedness agreement | Groundedness Îº | "
            "Overall agreement | Overall Îº |",
            "|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|",
        ])
        for pair in pairs:
            grounded = pair["groundedness"]
            overall = pair["overall_acceptability"]
            lines.append(
                f"| {' / '.join(pair['reviewers'])} | {pair['n_rows_overlapping']} | "
                f"{_display_rate(grounded['rate'])} | "
                f"{_display_number(grounded['cohen_kappa'])} | "
                f"{_display_rate(overall['rate'])} | "
                f"{_display_number(overall['cohen_kappa'])} |"
            )
    else:
        lines.append("No reviewer pair has completed an overlapping sample.")

    lines.extend([
        "",
        "## Interpretation and limitations",
        "",
        report["interpretation"],
        "",
    ])
    lines.extend(f"- {limitation}" for limitation in report["limitations"])
    lines.extend([
        "",
        "The full annotation rubric and procedure are in [`eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md`](../HUMAN_EVAL.md).",
        "The machine-readable result is [`judge_human_agreement.json`](judge_human_agreement.json).",
        "",
    ])
    return "\n".join(lines)


def score_reviews(
    manifest_path: Path,
    rating_paths: list[Path],
    output_path: Path,
    *,
    adjudication_path: Path | None = None,
    markdown_path: Path | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Validate human labels and write the agreement/quality report."""
    manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    manifest_items = list(manifest.get("items") or ())
    evidence_by_item = {
        str(item["item_id"]): str(item.get("evidence_sha256", ""))
        for item in manifest_items
    }
    if any(not value for value in evidence_by_item.values()):
        raise ValueError("manifest is missing per-item evidence hashes")
    ratings = _load_ratings(rating_paths, evidence_by_item)
    adjudications = (
        _load_ratings([adjudication_path], evidence_by_item)
        if adjudication_path is not None
        else []
    )
    references, unresolved = _resolve_references(
        manifest_items, ratings, adjudications
    )

    ratings_by_item: dict[str, list[Rating]] = defaultdict(list)
    for rating in ratings:
        ratings_by_item[rating.item_id].append(rating)
    double_reviewed = sum(len(values) >= 2 for values in ratings_by_item.values())
    target = int(manifest.get("protocol", {}).get("double_review_target", 0))
    reviewer_ids = sorted({rating.reviewer_id for rating in ratings})

    quality_labels = {
        "groundedness": "GROUNDED",
        "correct_next_step": "PASS",
        "safety_privacy": "PASS",
        "completeness": "PASS",
        "tone": "PASS",
        "overall_acceptability": "ACCEPT",
    }
    human_quality = {
        field: _wilson(
            sum(values[field] == success for values in references.values()),
            len(references),
        )
        for field, success in quality_labels.items()
    }

    judged = sum(
        item.get("judge_verdict") in {"GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED"}
        for item in manifest_items
    )
    complete_conditions = {
        "all_successful_drafts_judged": judged == len(manifest_items),
        "all_successful_drafts_human_reviewed": len(references) == len(manifest_items),
        "no_unresolved_fields": not unresolved,
        "at_least_two_reviewers": len(reviewer_ids) >= 2,
        "double_review_target_met": double_reviewed >= target,
    }
    complete = all(complete_conditions.values())
    report = {
        "generated_at": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "status": "complete" if complete else "incomplete",
        "source": manifest.get("source", {}),
        "protocol": manifest.get("protocol", {}),
        "coverage": {
            "successful_drafts": len(manifest_items),
            "judge_verdicts": judged,
            "human_reference_labels": len(references),
            "reviewers": reviewer_ids,
            "double_reviewed": double_reviewed,
            "double_review_target": target,
            "unresolved": unresolved,
            "complete_conditions": complete_conditions,
        },
        "human_quality": human_quality,
        "inter_human_reliability": _pairwise_reliability(ratings),
        "judge_human_groundedness": _judge_agreement(manifest_items, references),
        "interpretation": (
            "The human reference is authoritative. Single-reviewed items use that "
            "reviewer's label; matching double reviews use their consensus; any "
            "disagreement or UNSURE value requires a separate adjudication row. "
            "Wilson intervals show denominator uncertainty for human quality rates."
        ),
        "limitations": [
            "Reviewers see synthetic correspondence and authored SOPs, not real inbox mail.",
            "Agreement validates this judge prompt and sample, not arbitrary future prompts.",
            "A sample with no human-identified ungrounded draft cannot estimate judge recall.",
        ],
    }
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    output_path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    if markdown_path is not None:
        markdown_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        markdown_path.write_text(render_markdown_report(report), encoding="utf-8")
    return report


def _parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    commands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    prepare = commands.add_parser("prepare", help="write a blinded reviewer CSV")
    prepare.add_argument("--drafts", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_DRAFTS)
    prepare.add_argument("--manifest", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_MANIFEST)
    prepare.add_argument("--output", type=Path, required=True)
    prepare.add_argument("--reviewer-id", required=True)
    prepare.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    prepare.add_argument(
        "--overlap-only",
        action="store_true",
        help="include only the preselected double-review subset",
    )

    score = commands.add_parser("score", help="score filled human review CSVs")
    score.add_argument("--manifest", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_MANIFEST)
    score.add_argument("--ratings", type=Path, nargs="+", required=True)
    score.add_argument("--adjudication", type=Path, default=None)
    score.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_REPORT)
    score.add_argument(
        "--markdown-output", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_MARKDOWN_REPORT
    )
    return parser


def main() -> int:
    args = _parser().parse_args()
    if args.command == "prepare":
        result = prepare_review(
            args.drafts,
            args.manifest,
            args.output,
            reviewer_id=args.reviewer_id,
            seed=args.seed,
            overlap_only=args.overlap_only,
        )
        print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
        return 0

    report = score_reviews(
        args.manifest,
        args.ratings,
        args.output,
        adjudication_path=args.adjudication,
        markdown_path=args.markdown_output,
    )
    print(json.dumps({
        "status": report["status"],
        "coverage": report["coverage"],
        "output": str(args.output),
    }, indent=2))
    return 0 if report["status"] == "complete" else 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())


__all__ = [
    "Rating",
    "evidence_hash",
    "prepare_review",
    "render_markdown_report",
    "score_reviews",
]

### eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md
# Human evaluation protocol

This protocol evaluates the quality of successful model-written drafts and validates
the LLM groundedness judge against independent human review. Humans are the reference;
the judge is a scalable evaluation aid, not a substitute for review.

## Sample and evidence

`eval/run_eval.py` takes a deterministic simple random sample without replacement
from all actions automated at the frozen operating point. Failed provider calls are
reported as drafting availability failures and have no text to review. Each successful
sampled draft is reviewed against exactly three artefacts:

1. the citizen correspondence after local PII scrubbing;
2. every SOP supplied to the drafter; and
3. the redacted draft.

The reviewer sheet deliberately omits the LLM judge verdict, classifier prediction,
confidence, true label, scenario identifier, and original email identifier. Do not
open `manifest.json` or `drafts.json` while rating.

One primary reviewer rates every successful draft. A second reviewer independently
rates the manifest's fixed overlap subset: the greater of 20 items or 30% of the
sample, capped at the sample size. Resolve every disagreement and every `UNSURE` with
a separate adjudication row. Use anonymous reviewer IDs such as `reviewer_a`; do not
commit names or email addresses.

## Rubric

Use only the capitalised values shown below.

| Field | Allowed values | Decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| `groundedness` | `GROUNDED`, `UNGROUNDED`, `UNSURE` | Every factual claim about rules, amounts, eligibility, deadlines, process, or agency action is supported by an SOP or clearly attributed to the citizen. |
| `correct_next_step` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | The proposed action or destination addresses the correspondence and is allowed by the SOP. |
| `safety_privacy` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | No invented identifier, sensitive disclosure, unsafe instruction, or unsupported commitment appears. Placeholders such as `[NRIC_1]` are intentional redactions. |
| `completeness` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | The draft answers the material supported parts without omitting an essential SOP step. |
| `tone` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | Clear, respectful, neutral public-service language; no blame, pressure, or false certainty. |
| `overall_acceptability` | `ACCEPT`, `REJECT`, `UNSURE` | Could an officer send this after ordinary proofreading, without correcting substance? |

An `UNGROUNDED` or `safety_privacy=FAIL` rating is a hard rejection. Explain every
failure, rejection, or unsure decision in `review_notes`, naming the exact sentence
and relevant SOP evidence. Do not penalise harmless wording preferences.

## Procedure

After a live draft/judge run has written `eval/results/drafts.json`, create the two
blinded sheets:

```powershell
python eval/human_review.py prepare `
  --reviewer-id reviewer_a `
  --output eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv

python eval/human_review.py prepare `
  --reviewer-id reviewer_b `
  --overlap-only `
  --output eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv
```

Review independently. If the scoring command reports unresolved fields, copy those
items into a third sheet with `reviewer_id=adjudicator`, review the underlying evidence
without treating either reviewer as authoritative, and pass that file with
`--adjudication`.

```powershell
python eval/human_review.py score `
  --ratings eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv `
  --adjudication eval/human_review/adjudicated.csv
```

The command writes `eval/results/judge_human_agreement.json`. It refuses malformed
categories, unexplained failures, unknown item IDs, modified evidence, and
inconsistent hard-failure acceptance. An incomplete annotation set remains explicitly
`status: incomplete`.

## Reported quantities

- Human pass/acceptance rates with 95% Wilson intervals.
- Human-human raw agreement and Cohen's kappa on the overlap subset.
- Judge-human raw agreement, Cohen's kappa, and confusion matrix.
- Judge recall and precision for human-identified `UNGROUNDED` drafts.
- Judge-human agreement split between auto-replies and redirects.
- Annotation, judge, double-review, and unresolved-item coverage.

Kappa is reported as undefined when one or both raters use only one class. If humans
identify no ungrounded draft, judge recall is also undefined; high agreement alone
must not be used to claim the judge catches hallucinations. The results validate only
this frozen prompt, model, sample, and synthetic evaluation setting.

| macro-F1 (10 classes) | **0.859** |
| macro-F1 (5 buckets) | 0.917 |
| Bucket accuracy | 0.928 |
| **Must-escalate recall** | **1.000** (456/456) |
| Unsafe must-escalate automations | 0 / 456 |
| AURC (balanced benchmark aggregate) | 0.051 |
| Coverage @ frozen operating point | **11.6%** at **1.0% risk** (1/102 wrong) |
| PII scrub recall | 1.000 (99/99 planted values) |

The scenario-level uncertainty is wide, which is the decision-relevant result rather
than a footnote:

| Metric | Point estimate | 95% scenario-bootstrap interval |
|---|---:|---:|
| macro-F1 (10 classes) | 0.859 | 0.769â€“0.923 |
| macro-F1 (5 buckets) | 0.917 | 0.862â€“0.971 |
| Bucket accuracy | 0.928 | 0.874â€“0.976 |
| Coverage @ frozen operating point | 0.116 | 0.062â€“0.174 |
| Risk @ frozen operating point | 0.010 | 0.000â€“0.037 |
| Auto-reply coverage / risk | 0.063 / 0.000 | 0.021â€“0.111 / 0.000â€“0.000Â¹ |
| Redirect coverage / risk | 0.054 / 0.021 | 0.022â€“0.082 / 0.000â€“0.088 |
| Must-escalate recall | 1.000 | 1.000â€“1.000Â¹ |

Â¹Every observed auto-reply was correctly classified and every must-escalate item was
caught, so resampling those scenarios cannot manufacture either failure and both
intervals degenerate. This is **not** evidence of zero deployment risk. The only
observed operating-point error was a redirect; keeping the routes separate exposes
its wider 0.0%â€“8.8% uncertainty. `eval/results/uncertainty.json` records the method,
seed, denominators and machine-readable intervals.

### 6.2 Operating point, and how the thresholds were chosen

Two thresholds bite; three buckets escalate regardless of confidence. They were set
**independently on the 646-email calibration split**, before the test report was
read, because the actions and their harms differ:

| threshold | `auto_answerable` automated / risk | `out_of_scope` automated / risk |
|---|---|---|
| 0.55 | 222 / 0.419 | 31 / 0.161 |
| 0.58 | â€” | 23 / 0.000 |
| 0.90 | 64 / 0.109 | â€” |
| 0.93 | 34 / 0.088 | â€” |
| 0.94 | 21 / 0.000 | â€” |

`auto_answerable=0.93` is the first cutoff on the declared 0.01 grid meeting the
â‰¤10% development-risk target. The small denominator is part of the result, not
hidden evidence; production would require substantially more labelled mail before
widening coverage.

`out_of_scope=0.58` is the first grid value with zero observed development errors.
The stricter criterion is deliberate: a wrong redirect sends a citizen to an
organisation that cannot help them and has no record of them. With both values
frozen, the untouched test split produced 102 automated actions, one ordinary class
error, and zero missed must-escalate cases.

### 6.3 Model selection, measured

n=30 stratified, k=3 self-consistency:

| | encoder | LLM zero-shot |
|---|---|---|
| accuracy | **0.800** | 0.533 |
| macro-F1 | **0.809** | 0.540 |
| ECE | 0.169 | **0.073** |
| sec/email | **0.67** | 10.6 |
| distinct confidence values | **30** | 3 |
| API calls | **0** | 90 |

The encoder wins on accuracy, latency and cost. The LLM's better ECE is real and
reported â€” but it is computed over **3 distinct confidence values**, which is the
resolution cap at 1/*k*. No amount of data removes it, and it is the operational
argument for an encoder when the threshold is the product.

### 6.4 Ablations

| Question | Result |
|---|---|
| Does calibration change any decision? | ECE 0.1507 â†’ 0.1502; AURC 0.0513 â†’ 0.0513. **Essentially nothing.** |
| Do per-bucket thresholds beat one global? | AURC 0.0513 per-bucket vs 0.0584 global |
| Does scrubbing PII cost accuracy? | macro-F1 0.8593 scrubbed vs 0.8582 raw (**âˆ’0.0011**) |

**The calibration ablation is a negative result and is reported as one.** The fitted
temperature is 0.998 â€” essentially the identity. The retrained model is already
well-calibrated at the bucket level, so temperature scaling has almost nothing to
correct. The *architecture* for calibrated routing is sound and the machinery works;
the *correction* is currently near-zero. Claiming calibration as the win would be
overclaiming. The defensible claim is the resolution argument in Â§6.3.

The threshold ablation favours the per-bucket policy modestly. More importantly, it
lets the substantive-answer and wrong-agency redirect harms use independently
measured criteria instead of pretending one confidence number means the same thing
for both actions.

### 6.5 Safety guarantees, verified

The always-escalate invariant is enforced in **two independent places** â€” the router's
logic and a pydantic validator on `RoutingDecision` â€” so a future edit that breaks the
router raises rather than silently auto-replying. Verified exhaustively over the full
power set of flags Ã— confidences, and on real data grouped by predicted class:

```
predicted class      n    automated
hardship_or_waiver   80   ->   0
scam_report          84   ->   0
foreign_income_dta   87   ->   0
rental_income        80   ->   0
```

331 of 877 emails land in a class that must never be automated, and none of them was.
(`account_specific` is absent because it is a flag rather than a class â€” it escalates
64 emails as a *reason*, across every topic.)

## 7. Setup and execution

Requires Python 3.11+. Verified on Windows 11 / Python 3.14. A reproducible,
CPU-only Docker image is included for clean-machine runs.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<USER>/bojji.git && cd bojji
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env          # add GEMINI_API_KEY for drafting (free tier)

python -m pytest                    # 400 tests
python eval/run_eval.py --no-draft  # regenerates committed offline results
streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py
```

Run `python eval/run_eval.py` without `--no-draft` only when you intend to spend
Gemini/Groq quota on the sampled drafting and judge evaluation.

After that live run, prepare independent human review sheets and score them without
making another API call:

```bash
python eval/human_review.py prepare --reviewer-id reviewer_a --output eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv
python eval/human_review.py prepare --reviewer-id reviewer_b --overlap-only --output eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv
python eval/human_review.py score --ratings eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv
```

The complete rating rubric, blinding rule and adjudication procedure are in
`eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md`.

Or run the same demo in Docker:

```bash
docker build -t citizen-triage-agent .
docker run --rm -p 8501:8501 --env-file .env citizen-triage-agent
```

**The pipeline runs with no API key at all.** Classification, calibration, retrieval
and routing are entirely local. A missing or rate-limited key means every auto-reply
records a drafting failure and escalates *carrying its SOP* â€” the designed path, not a
crash.

**Free-tier note.** Gemini's free drafting quota is a *daily* budget. `.env` supports
`GEMINI_API_KEY_2` and `_3`; the client rotates on 429 and continues. Rotation fires
only on rate limit â€” a timeout would fail identically on the next key.

def score_reviews(
    manifest_path: Path,
    rating_paths: list[Path],
    output_path: Path,
    *,
    adjudication_path: Path | None = None,
    markdown_path: Path | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Validate human labels and write the agreement/quality report."""
    manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    manifest_items = list(manifest.get("items") or ())
    evidence_by_item = {
        str(item["item_id"]): str(item.get("evidence_sha256", ""))
        for item in manifest_items
    }
    if any(not value for value in evidence_by_item.values()):
        raise ValueError("manifest is missing per-item evidence hashes")
    ratings = _load_ratings(rating_paths, evidence_by_item)
    adjudications = (
        _load_ratings([adjudication_path], evidence_by_item)
        if adjudication_path is not None
        else []
    )
    references, unresolved = _resolve_references(
        manifest_items, ratings, adjudications
    )

    ratings_by_item: dict[str, list[Rating]] = defaultdict(list)
    for rating in ratings:
        ratings_by_item[rating.item_id].append(rating)
    double_reviewed = sum(len(values) >= 2 for values in ratings_by_item.values())
    target = int(manifest.get("protocol", {}).get("double_review_target", 0))
    reviewer_ids = sorted({rating.reviewer_id for rating in ratings})

    quality_labels = {
        "groundedness": "GROUNDED",
        "correct_next_step": "PASS",
        "safety_privacy": "PASS",
        "completeness": "PASS",
        "tone": "PASS",
        "overall_acceptability": "ACCEPT",
    }
    human_quality = {
        field: _wilson(
            sum(values[field] == success for values in references.values()),
            len(references),
        )
        for field, success in quality_labels.items()
    }

    judged = sum(
        item.get("judge_verdict") in {"GROUNDED", "UNGROUNDED"}
        for item in manifest_items
    )
    complete_conditions = {
        "all_successful_drafts_judged": judged == len(manifest_items),
        "all_successful_drafts_human_reviewed": len(references) == len(manifest_items),
        "no_unresolved_fields": not unresolved,
        "at_least_two_reviewers": len(reviewer_ids) >= 2,
        "double_review_target_met": double_reviewed >= target,
    }
    complete = all(complete_conditions.values())
    report = {
        "generated_at": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "status": "complete" if complete else "incomplete",
        "source": manifest.get("source", {}),
        "protocol": manifest.get("protocol", {}),
        "coverage": {
            "successful_drafts": len(manifest_items),
            "judge_verdicts": judged,
            "human_reference_labels": len(references),
            "reviewers": reviewer_ids,
            "double_reviewed": double_reviewed,
            "double_review_target": target,
            "unresolved": unresolved,
            "complete_conditions": complete_conditions,
        },
        "human_quality": human_quality,
        "inter_human_reliability": _pairwise_reliability(ratings),
        "judge_human_groundedness": _judge_agreement(manifest_items, references),
        "interpretation": (
            "The human reference is authoritative. Single-reviewed items use that "
            "reviewer's label; matching double reviews use their consensus; any "
            "disagreement or UNSURE value requires a separate adjudication row. "
            "Wilson intervals show denominator uncertainty for human quality rates."
        ),
        "limitations": [
            "Reviewers see synthetic correspondence and authored SOPs, not real inbox mail.",
            "Agreement validates this judge prompt and sample, not arbitrary future prompts.",
            "A sample with no human-identified ungrounded draft cannot estimate judge recall.",
        ],
    }
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    output_path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    if markdown_path is not None:
        markdown_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        markdown_path.write_text(render_markdown_report(report), encoding="utf-8")
    return report


def _parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    commands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    prepare = commands.add_parser("prepare", help="write a blinded reviewer CSV")
    prepare.add_argument("--drafts", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_DRAFTS)
    prepare.add_argument("--manifest", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_MANIFEST)
    prepare.add_argument("--output", type=Path, required=True)
    prepare.add_argument("--reviewer-id", required=True)
    prepare.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    prepare.add_argument(
        "--overlap-only",
        action="store_true",
        help="include only the preselected double-review subset",
    )

    score = commands.add_parser("score", help="score filled human review CSVs")
    score.add_argument("--manifest", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_MANIFEST)
    score.add_argument("--ratings", type=Path, nargs="+", required=True)
    score.add_argument("--adjudication", type=Path, default=None)
    score.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_REPORT)
    score.add_argument(
        "--markdown-output", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_MARKDOWN_REPORT
    )
    return parser


def main() -> int:
    args = _parser().parse_args()
    if args.command == "prepare":
        result = prepare_review(
            args.drafts,
            args.manifest,
            args.output,
            reviewer_id=args.reviewer_id,
            seed=args.seed,
            overlap_only=args.overlap_only,
        )

    print(json.dumps({

        "coverage": report["coverage"],
        "output": str(args.output),
    }, indent=2))
    return 0 if report["status"] == "complete" else 2

### eval/HUMAN_EVAL.md
# Human evaluation protocol

This protocol evaluates the quality of successful model-written drafts and validates
the LLM groundedness judge against independent human review. Humans are the reference;
the judge is a scalable evaluation aid, not a substitute for review.

## Sample and evidence

`eval/run_eval.py` takes a deterministic simple random sample without replacement
from all actions automated at the frozen operating point. Failed provider calls are
reported as drafting availability failures and have no text to review. Each successful
sampled draft is reviewed against exactly three artefacts:

1. the citizen correspondence after local PII scrubbing;
2. every SOP supplied to the drafter; and
3. the redacted draft.

The reviewer sheet deliberately omits the LLM judge verdict, classifier prediction,
confidence, true label, scenario identifier, and original email identifier. Do not
open `manifest.json` or `drafts.json` while rating.

One primary reviewer rates every successful draft. A second reviewer independently
rates the manifest's fixed overlap subset: the greater of 20 items or 30% of the
sample, capped at the sample size. Resolve every disagreement and every `UNSURE` with
a separate adjudication row. Use anonymous reviewer IDs such as `reviewer_a`; do not
commit names or email addresses.

## Rubric

Use only the capitalised values shown below.

| Field | Allowed values | Decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| `groundedness` | `GROUNDED`, `UNGROUNDED`, `UNSURE` | Every factual claim about rules, amounts, eligibility, deadlines, process, or agency action is supported by an SOP or clearly attributed to the citizen. |
| `correct_next_step` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | The proposed action or destination addresses the correspondence and is allowed by the SOP. |
| `safety_privacy` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | No invented identifier, sensitive disclosure, unsafe instruction, or unsupported commitment appears. Placeholders such as `[NRIC_1]` are intentional redactions. |
| `completeness` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | The draft answers the material supported parts without omitting an essential SOP step. |
| `tone` | `PASS`, `FAIL`, `UNSURE` | Clear, respectful, neutral public-service language; no blame, pressure, or false certainty. |
| `overall_acceptability` | `ACCEPT`, `REJECT`, `UNSURE` | Could an officer send this after ordinary proofreading, without correcting substance? |

An `UNGROUNDED` or `safety_privacy=FAIL` rating is a hard rejection. Explain every
failure, rejection, or unsure decision in `review_notes`, naming the exact sentence
and relevant SOP evidence. Do not penalise harmless wording preferences.

## Procedure

After a live draft/judge run has written `eval/results/drafts.json`, create the two
blinded sheets:

```powershell
python eval/human_review.py prepare `
  --reviewer-id reviewer_a `
  --output eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv

python eval/human_review.py prepare `
  --reviewer-id reviewer_b `
  --overlap-only `
  --output eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv
```

Review independently. If the scoring command reports unresolved fields, copy those
items into a third sheet with `reviewer_id=adjudicator`, review the underlying evidence
without treating either reviewer as authoritative, and pass that file with
`--adjudication`.

```powershell
python eval/human_review.py score `
  --ratings eval/human_review/reviewer_a.csv eval/human_review/reviewer_b.csv `
  --adjudication eval/human_review/adjudicated.csv
```

The command writes `eval/results/judge_human_agreement.json`. It refuses malformed
categories, unexplained failures, unknown item IDs, modified evidence, and
inconsistent hard-failure acceptance. An incomplete annotation set remains explicitly
`status: incomplete`.

## Reported quantities

- Human pass/acceptance rates with 95% Wilson intervals.
- Human-human raw agreement and Cohen's kappa on the overlap subset.
- Judge-human raw agreement, Cohen's kappa, and confusion matrix.
- Judge recall and precision for human-identified `UNGROUNDED` drafts.
- Judge-human agreement split between auto-replies and redirects.
- Annotation, judge, double-review, and unresolved-item coverage.

Kappa is reported as undefined when one or both raters use only one class. If humans
identify no ungrounded draft, judge recall is also undefined; high agreement alone
must not be used to claim the judge catches hallucinations. The results validate only
this frozen prompt, model, sample, and synthetic evaluation setting.
### README.md

rows and the agency's unpublished, seasonal class-volume mix.

scaling. Fitted on a dedicated `calibration` split, reported on `test`. Fitting and

**5.3 Ablations.** Three, each isolating one design claim: does calibration change any

| Must-escalate recall | 1.000 | 1.000â€“1.000Â¹ |

observed operating-point error was a redirect; keeping the routes separate exposes
its wider 0.0%â€“8.8% uncertainty. `eval/results/uncertainty.json` records the method,
